text: Every night, one man in the cell describes an old movie out loud, scene by scene, to his cellmate, a journalist being tortured for his politics. Molina dressed shop windows for a living and carries a memory full of romances. Valentin regards all of it as sentimental waste and is not in a position to leave the room. Héctor Babenco builds two hours almost entirely out of that arrangement: two bodies, one cell, and a voice conjuring pictures no camera in the room will ever show. The stakes are not escape. They are what the telling costs the teller, and what becomes of a man who has decided that pleasure is a luxury politics cannot afford. Brazilian, made in 1985, performed in English, and held on Abraccine's list of the hundred best Brazilian films.

At the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, a sideshow barker gets the better of his more successful neighbour and walks off with the man's girlfriend as well. That pattern is the film. Florenz Ziegfeld makes a fortune, spends it on a show, loses it, and begins again at a larger scale, with the same rival always somewhere nearby to be measured against. Robert Z. Leonard has three hours and five minutes, and uses them the way a life uses decades: repetition, with the stakes raised each time round. The production numbers are staged at a size that only makes sense as argument, since a story about a man ruined by the scale of his revues has to show the revues, or the ruin is only bookkeeping. What accumulates is less a portrait of showmanship than of an appetite that never learns anything.

The tennis matters more than it looks: young people in whites, a private court, a high wall around it. Inside, a wealthy Jewish family keeps the season going, with friends invited, parties held, the calendar honoured. Outside, Fascist Italy is tightening the laws that decide what such a family may keep. Vittorio De Sica gives this ninety-five minutes, brief for a story measured in years, and the compression shows in what he selects: manners rather than incident, who is asked in and who quietly stops coming, what gets said at the table and what is put off until later. His material is the arithmetic by which comfortable people persuade themselves they are the exception. Berlin gave it the Golden Bear; the Academy, its award for a film in another language.

Seventy-six minutes, one play, and a cast who cannot leave the building when rehearsal ends. The men are inmates of a prison in Rome and the play is Julius Caesar, in which friends talk themselves into a killing. Filed as documentary and as drama, the film declines to settle which it is, and the refusal is method rather than evasion: a speech about what a man owes the people closest to him is a different speech in this room, spoken by these readers. What it watches is the work itself. Lines learned, lines argued over, a text handled by men who did not choose it and are in no position to treat it as literature. Berlin gave it the Golden Bear, and Italy its David di Donatello for best film and best director.

Two hundred francs, handed to a man sleeping under a Paris bridge by a stranger who wants the money repaid to a church rather than to himself. Andreas Kartak intends to pay. Ermanno Olmi then spends a little over two hours on an errand a sober man could finish in an afternoon, and the gap between those two durations is the film: a debt nobody is enforcing, owed to nobody who will check, kept alive entirely by the debtor's insistence that it is real. Drink interferes. So do circumstances, which arrive often enough to become their own kind of trouble. Venice answered with the Golden Lion and Italy with the David di Donatello for best film, for a picture whose whole dramatic question is whether one man keeps a promise made to a stranger.

A lawyer arrives in a small mountain town to explain to grieving parents that someone must be at fault, and that fault can be converted into money. More than a dozen children are dead after a school bus leaves the road. The town has not finished working out how to hold itself together when the class action begins sorting neighbours into clients and obstacles, and Atom Egoyan is far more interested in that sorting than in the crash: the visits, the careful account each household gives of a morning nobody wants to describe twice. What is at stake is not the verdict. It is whether a place survives being asked, one kitchen at a time, to turn its dead into evidence. Cannes answered with the Grand Prix, and TIFF has it among the ten best Canadian films ever made.

There are four daughters in the house, and the young deserter their father takes in likes all of them. The year is 1931, the country Spain, and Manolo welcomes the runaway soldier on the strength of his politics, which indicates the kind of household this will be: one where the rules being fought over everywhere else are, for a season, simply set aside. Fernando Trueba plays that suspension for warmth rather than satire. The soldier has to choose, and each sister makes him a different offer, not of herself only but of the man he would have to become to be worth her. The comedy runs on his inability to refuse any of it. The Academy gave it the award for a film in another language, and Caimán keeps it on its hundred best Spanish films.

Stephen has tenure at Oxford, a wife, a settled life, and no appetite left for any of it. Then there is Anna, engaged to one of his students, and he discovers an appetite after all, though he would call it interest, or concern, or almost anything else. Joseph Losey keeps the surfaces calm: the college, the house, the weekend hospitality, the English arrangement under which the least revealing thing a man does is the thing he admits to. A car crash binds the three of them together, and the film works backwards through it rather than towards it, so the question is never what happened. It is which of them will say what he wanted, and to whom, and how long the saying can be put off. Cannes gave it the Grand Prix.

A film crew on the Portuguese coast has run out of stock, and nobody has come to tell them what happens next. They were shooting their own version of a 1956 Roger Corman picture about the end of the world; now the production has quietly stopped existing around them while they wait for a producer no one can find. Wim Wenders lets that waiting run a long time before Munro, the director, goes looking. The search turns out to be less a rescue than an audit of what a film costs the people making it. There is a joke buried in the setup, and it has teeth: the story they abandoned was about survivors rationing what is left, and the crew has become precisely that. Venice gave it the Golden Lion; the German Film Award named it best feature.

The parish is poor, the house is plain, and the woman who moved into it was raised for something else entirely. Henrik studies for the priesthood on almost nothing; Anna's family has never had to think about money. They marry across that difference, go to the country, and find that class is not an obstacle a couple clears once but a fault that keeps generating fresh arguments, each of them reasonable, each worse than the one before. Bille August takes three hours over it, which is about right for a quarrel with no single cause. And the film's other subject sits just outside the frame: these two become the parents of Ingmar Bergman, which makes the ordinary weather of their marriage a matter of some consequence. Cannes gave it the Palme d'Or, and its award for best actress.

The defendants are judges, which means the trial cannot simply be about men who broke the law. In 1947 a military tribunal sits to hear charges against four Germans who served on the bench under the Nazi regime: men who signed, sentenced and interpreted, in rooms not unlike the one they now stand in. Stanley Kramer spends three hours and eleven minutes almost entirely on speech. Whether that is a limitation or the argument depends on the weight given to hearing an intelligent defence made well, and Hans Rolfe is handed a real case to make. Chief Justice Haywood must set it against a general's widow, an American captain, and a witness who would rather not be there. It sits in the National Film Registry.

Two people fall in love at first sight, and both of them kill for a living. Charley Partanna works for the Prizzis, one of the richest crime families in the country, and has never found the job difficult until the woman he wants turns out to be freelance in the same trade. John Huston plays this as comedy and keeps the temperature low: the family conducts its affairs with the ledgers and grievances of any old firm, so Charley's trouble is procedural before it is moral. He is loyal. He is slow. He believes the arithmetic can be made to come out. Watching a competent man learn that his two allegiances cannot both be served, and be the last in the room to notice, is the whole of it. New York's critics named it the best film of its year.

Carmen wants the one man on the post who is not already looking at her, and he has orders to leave. She makes parachutes; Joe is engaged to Cindy Lou and bound for pilot training and a war in Korea, and the film's tension is how little any of that turns out to weigh. The camp supplies the walls: ranks, engagements, orders, a closed world in which everyone knows what everyone else is meant to do next. Otto Preminger shot it in 1954 as a full musical with an all-Black cast, which is part of what the picture is doing rather than a footnote to it. It moves at the speed of appetite. Carmen is written as a woman who declines to serve as a warning, and her songs are arguments, not decoration. It sits now in the National Film Registry.

Roberto's first child is days old when he crosses the border north to look for work. What follows is less a journey than an accounting: what the work pays, who takes a share before it reaches him, how much of a wage survives the distance between a field and the household it was meant to reach. The finding, arrived at over ninety-six minutes rather than announced, is that effort is not the variable. Roberto works, and works, and the sum does not move. Robert M. Young made it in 1978 and pitched it at the level of hours put in and rates paid, which is where the pressure actually lives. Cannes gave it the Caméra d'Or, San Sebastián the Golden Shell, and the National Film Registry has since taken it in.
